citation: Acceptability of a fee for home delivery of HIV treatment in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa (2024). BMC Health Services Research 24. doi:10.1186/s12913-023-10533-4
Barriers to care among people living with HIV in South Africa: patient and healthcare provider perspectives (2012). AIDS Care. Durban, fieldwork around 2010; patient accounts only.

A qualitative study of the social and structural vulnerabilities of HIV and chronic disease syndemics in low-resource urban health facilities in South Africa (2026). Discover Public Health. doi:10.1186/s12982-026-01850-0

claims.text: Being seen at a clinic or identified as HIV-positive is the binding threat: fear of judgment and disclosure through clinic attendance drives avoidance of collection, so a delivery option is judged by whether it removes visibility from queues and clinic spaces.
evaluative_rules: Judge a collection option by whether it hides your status from people who know you, not by convenience alone
objections: Will using this expose me to people who know me or let them identify my status?
vocabulary: scared to be seen in the clinic queues
claims.about: HIV treatment or testing (ARVs, PrEP), where being seen collecting it at a clinic could reveal your status

readings.text: Someone who fears being seen in clinic queues would weigh a delivery option mainly by whether it removes them from those visible spaces.

If a person is worried about being seen by people they know at the clinic, they would judge a delivery option by whether it avoids those encounters, but may still fear being seen receiving medication at home.

claims.text: Disclosure risk travels home: visible or identifiable delivery threatens secrecy with household members, partners, and neighbours, so home delivery is judged acceptable only when it is designed to conceal HIV status.
evaluative_rules: Judge a delivery service by whether it can be seen or recognised as HIV-related by people at home
objections: Will the delivery be branded, uniformed, or repeated in a way that reveals my secret to my household or neighbours?
vocabulary: my privacy or secret might be exposed
a car that is not branded
claims.about: medication or treatment delivered to your home, where household members or neighbours could see it

readings.text: Someone who has not told their parents or partner they are taking medication would weigh a new delivery service mainly by whether the delivery itself could expose that secret, so any visible sign of medication would make it unacceptable.

If a person believes a delivery is too obvious because a uniformed worker or branded car signals that someone in the house is sick, they would be more open to a service that uses an unbranded car and no uniform.

Someone who has paused treatment at home for fear of disclosure would judge a new delivery option by whether it could be noticed by household members or neighbours, and would likely reject any service that draws attention to the home.

If a person fears a partner's reaction or loss of support, they would weigh a new delivery service primarily by whether it could be kept hidden from that partner, and would only consider it if it could be made to look like something other than HIV care.

claims.text: Money is already spoken for: when income is absent and essential food competes with every fee, any charge is weighed against household survival, so a fee-based delivery is acceptable only if it replaces an existing clinic cost or is pooled and shared.
evaluative_rules: Judge a fee by whether it takes money away from food and survival, not by its face value
objections: Will paying for this mean my household goes without food or I must beg or borrow to cover it?
vocabulary: the same money is the one we need to buy healthy food
any amount will be a problem for an unemployed person

readings.text: Someone who says the same money is needed to buy healthy food would weigh any delivery fee against whether it removes an existing clinic cost like transport or a return visit, not as a new expense.

If a person fears they would have to sell scrap metal or steal gates and pots to raise cash for a delivery, they would see a fee-based service as a threat to household survival unless the fee is pooled and shared.

Someone who already missed a clinic appointment because they could not raise two hundred Rand would be more open to a delivery only if it clearly replaces that clinic cost and does not add a new charge.

If a person weighs a twenty Rand lettuce against a loaf of bread for a child, they would treat any delivery fee as competing with essential food and would accept it only when it is shared or substitutes an existing clinic expense.

claims.text: Clinic time is lost income: when visits consume a full day and employers are inflexible, the cost of attending is counted in wages and queues, so a delivery fee is judged worthwhile when it is set against what a clinic visit already costs.
evaluative_rules: Judge a delivery fee against the time, travel, and lost work of a clinic visit, not as a new expense
objections: Does the fee cost me less than the day of work and transport I would lose at the clinic?
vocabulary: holding a queue at the clinic

readings.text: Someone who says they would rather pay for delivery than hold a queue at the clinic would weigh a delivery fee against the wages and time already lost to a full-day visit.
If a person must negotiate with an employer just to attend on a different day, they would judge a delivery fee as worthwhile when it removes that negotiation and the risk of being refused.
Someone who already pays transport to go to other clinics would weigh a delivery fee favourably only if it is set at a similar expense to what a clinic visit already costs.
If a person compares work and the clinic and decides not to go back because they cannot miss work, they would weigh a delivery fee against the income they would otherwise lose by attending.

claims.text: Continuity is the goal: convenience and flexibility matter because missed appointments and clinic delays break treatment, so delivery is judged acceptable when it is linked to clinical check-ups and affordable group payment arrangements.
evaluative_rules: Judge a delivery scheme by whether it keeps medication flowing without breaking the link to clinical monitoring
objections: Will this still get me my blood check-ups and medication on time, or will I fall through the cracks?

readings.text: Someone who values getting medication at home even when busy would weigh a new delivery option by whether it removes the need to go to the pharmacy and find medication has not yet arrived.
If delivery is offered, someone would weigh it by whether it is linked to clinics or hospitals for annual check-ups and blood check-ups rather than being delivery alone.
Someone who sees group contribution as a way to raise the delivery amount would weigh a new option by whether it allows group collection and payment among fellow group mates.

If a new option is introduced, someone would weigh it by whether it eliminates concerns around missed appointments through the convenience and flexibility of getting medication even with other commitments.

region: KwaZulu-Natal, Durban and Johannesburg, South Africa
confidence: Three qualitative South African studies of people living with HIV at public clinics: two focus groups of 20 on a proposed fee for home delivery of treatment, 51 patients in Durban (patient accounts only), and 13 patients in Johannesburg. Low-income, uninsured; the HIV-disclosure findings reach only pitches about HIV treatment or home delivery.
subject: paying for care or for convenience without medical aid: fees weighed against food and wages, a day lost in the queue, and being seen at the clinic
year_note: Durban around 2010; KwaZulu-Natal focus groups 2019 (published 2024); Johannesburg 2024.
borrowed_from: Low-income people living with HIV at public clinics, weighing fees against food, wages, time and being seen. Comfortable people without medical aid hear it from people close to them; no study of them exists yet.
